readerTitle: Why the second booking matters more than the first
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Homejoy, 미국 가정 청소 플랫폼, 2015년 폐업) + 가상 적용 (청소 서비스, 포장재 제조사, 리텐션 곡선 수치)
insight: 첫 구매는 할인과 광고로 살 수 있지만, 고객이 스스로 다시 돌아오는 것은 살 수 없다. 그래서 제품-시장 적합성의 진짜 신호는 가입 수가 아니라 재구매다.
misconception: 가입자와 첫 주문이 빠르게 늘면 시장이 제품을 원한다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: Huet, E. (2015). What Really Killed Homejoy? It Couldn't Hold On To Its Customers. Forbes.
Homejoy 폐업 보도 (2015년 7월, TechCrunch 등). 회사는 청소원의 고용 형태를 둘러싼 소송을 이유로 들었습니다.
리텐션 곡선 수치와 청소·포장재 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Homejoy의 폐업 시점(2015년 7월)과 회사가 밝힌 공식 이유(청소원 근로자 분류 소송)를 게시 전에 당시 보도로 다시 확인하세요.
첫 청소 대폭 할인, 낮은 재예약률, 고객이 청소원과 직접 거래한 문제는 Forbes(2015) 등 보도에 근거한 내용입니다. 정확한 할인 가격과 재예약률 수치는 확실하지 않아 카드에 넣지 않았고 "reportedly"로 표시했습니다.
차트 수치는 가상입니다. A: 100→35→12→4%, B: 100→55→44→42%. B는 4개월 이후 거의 평평해지는 모양을 보여주기 위한 값입니다.
8번 카드: 처음 20개 고객 중 12곳 재주문 = 60%. 계산 확인 완료.

cards.title: Why the second booking matters more than the first
body: In the early 2010s, Homejoy let people book a home cleaning online in a minute. It raised tens of millions of dollars and expanded to cities across the US and beyond.
First bookings poured in. By 2015, the company was gone. The warning sign had been there early, in the bookings that never came.

image.label: A cleaner's calendar full of first visits and empty repeat slots
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 큰 달력에 첫 방문 칸은 초록 스티커로 가득하고, 그 다음 달 재방문 칸은 거의 비어 있음. 청소 도구 바구니가 옆에 놓임. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Is your cleaning service working?
body: You launched a home cleaning service three months ago. You need to tell an investor whether customers really want it.
Which number do you trust most?

options.feedback: Fast growth looks great, but first bookings can be bought with ads and discounts. It shows interest, not whether the service is worth paying for again.
Happy customers are a good start. But people rate a nice visit highly and still never book again.

options.text: The share of first-time customers who book again at full price within two months
options.feedback: Coming back without a push is hard to fake. It shows the service solved a real need well enough to pay for twice.

cards.title: Lots of first visits. Too few second ones.
body: Homejoy grew quickly with deep discounts on the first cleaning. Reporting at the time described what came next: many customers tried it once and reportedly never booked again.
Some who did like their cleaner reportedly hired them directly, outside the platform. When Homejoy shut down in July 2015, it pointed to lawsuits over whether cleaners should be employees.
But the growth had depended on constantly buying new customers, because too few of the old ones stayed.

cards.title: Retention is the real signal
body: **Retention** is the share of customers who keep buying from you over time, on their own, without a special push.

Here is why it matters for product-market fit. You can buy a first purchase with ads, promotions and a good pitch. A second purchase is much harder to buy. It happens mostly when the product actually did its job.

image.label: A crowd entering a door, a smaller group returning through it
image.brief: 가게 문 앞 일러스트. 왼쪽에는 "First purchase" 라벨과 함께 많은 사람이 할인 풍선을 따라 들어가고, 오른쪽에는 "Came back" 라벨과 함께 적은 사람이 스스로 다시 걸어 들어옴. 따뜻한 색감.

cards.title: Look for the curve that flattens.
body: Follow everyone who first bought in the same month. Business A loses almost all of them. Business B loses many early, then the line levels off.
That flat part is the signal: a core group that keeps coming back. Some early drop-off is normal. A line that keeps falling toward zero is not.
cards.softwareNote: For apps, this is the classic retention curve: the share of users from one signup month still active weeks later. A curve that flattens above zero is one of the clearest early signs of fit, whatever the signup numbers say.

image.label: Two retention curves: dying vs flattening
image.brief: Retention infographic. Shop A line keeps falling 100-35-12-4. Shop B falls then flattens 100-55-44-42.

cards.title: Measure at your customers' natural rhythm.
body: What counts as "coming back" depends on how often people need you. A cleaning service might expect a booking every few weeks. A dentist, every six months.
Some businesses are rarely bought twice, like a roof or a wedding photographer. There, the return looks different: referrals, reviews and customers sending friends.
The question stays the same: after trying it, do people choose you again?

cards.title: Retention can be faked too.
body: Long contracts, high switching costs and renewal discounts can keep customers who would leave if they could. That's lock-in, not fit.
One big customer can also hide many small ones walking away. Check retention by group and by customer count, not just total revenue.
Ask yourself: **would they stay if leaving were easy?**

cards.title: Now it's a packaging maker.
body: You make custom shipping boxes for small online brands. After your first year, you have three pieces of good news. Which one best shows that customers really need what you make?

options.text: 80 trial orders after a trade show
options.feedback: It shows the pitch works. But trial orders are like first bookings: they tell you nothing yet about whether the boxes earn a second order.

options.text: 12 of your first 20 customers reordered at full price, without a sales call
options.feedback: Sixty percent came back on their own. That's the hardest signal to fake, and it's built from real buying decisions.

options.text: One distributor signed a two-year contract for half your volume
options.feedback: Valuable revenue, but a contract holds the customer in place. It also hides whether smaller buyers would choose you again.

cards.title: Growth shows interest. Retention shows fit.
body: New customers can be bought. Customers who come back by choice tell you the product works.
**Try it today:** take the customers who first bought from you three months ago. Count how many have bought again without a discount or a nudge.
